explain.say: Your body is about 60 percent water and loses some all day through breathing, sweating and urine. Thirst is the alarm that tells you to top it up.

explain.say: As you lose water, your blood becomes slightly saltier. Special sensor cells in the hypothalamus of the brain detect this change.

explain.say: The brain then does two things. It makes you feel thirsty, and it releases a hormone called ADH, which tells the kidneys to put more water back into the blood and make less urine.

faq.q: How does the body know it needs water?
faq.a: Sensor cells in the hypothalamus detect when the blood gets too salty, and sensors in the heart and blood vessels detect when blood volume drops. Either can trigger thirst.
asks: Tell me about the brain sensors firing

faq.a: ADH, antidiuretic hormone, is released from the base of the brain when the body is short of water. It makes the kidneys return more water to the blood, so urine becomes darker and smaller in amount.
asks: Tell me about thirst and ADH

faq.q: Why does salty food make you thirsty?
faq.a: Salt goes into your blood and makes it saltier. The brain's sensors detect it and make you thirsty, so you drink water to bring the saltiness back to normal.
asks: Why do crisps make me thirsty?

faq.q: Why does thirst stop before the water is absorbed?
faq.a: Swallowing and a filling stomach send quick signals to the brain that switch thirst off early, before the water has fully reached the blood. It stops you drinking far too much.
asks: Why do I stop feeling thirsty right after drinking?

faq.q: How much of the body is water?
faq.a: An adult body is roughly 50 to 60 percent water, and a baby's is even more.
asks: What percent of us is water?

facts: The adult human body is about 50 to 60 percent water.
ADH, also called vasopressin, makes the kidneys reabsorb more water.
